title: Musa and the shepherd
hookLine: Musa rebukes a shepherd's simple prayer, and is told Allah looks at the heart, not the words (Masnavi 2)
tomorrow: everyone's touching the same elephant. why do they disagree?

cards: Bedtime, and a little kid squeezes his eyes shut: dear God, thanks for my dog, and for pizza, and please fix Grandma's knee, and do You have a dog? The grown-ups in the doorway try not to laugh.

Rumi tells a story about a prayer like that. A shepherd sits on a hillside, talking out loud to God: where are You, so I can sew Your shoes and comb Your hair, wash Your clothes, bring You milk, kiss Your hands?
And a prophet is walking by and hears every word. It's Musa, Moses. He stops.

teach.b: Musa rounds on the shepherd. Who are you talking to? God has no body; He needs no milk and no shoes.
Talk like that is an insult. The shepherd tears his shirt in shame and runs off into the desert. Then the revelation comes to Musa, and it's a rebuke.
Paraphrased: you have separated My servant from Me.

teach.h: SENT TO UNITE, NOT TO CUT OFF.
teach.b: You were sent to bring people together, not to cut them off. I don't look at the tongue and the words; I look at the heart and its state. Musa runs after the shepherd, finds him, and tells him: there are no rules for you.
Say whatever your heart says. Here's what makes the story more than sweet. Musa wasn't wrong about God.
The Qur'an itself says there is nothing like Him. His theology was right, and his timing and tone cut a man off from God.
The story keeps both: right belief matters, and correction must never sever.
Its center has a hadith behind it, in Sahih Muslim: God does not look at your bodies or your appearance, but at your hearts and your deeds. The shepherd's words were clumsy. His heart was burning.

how: Alongside the set words of the daily prayer, Muslims make dua, personal prayer, in any language and their own words; teachers use Musa and the shepherd to warn against shaming sincere but clumsy prayer.

games.q: what does “musa and the shepherd” mean?
o: only exact, formal words reach God
sincere words from the heart reach God
a prophet's prayers count more than others'

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: sent to unite, not to cut off
God looks at hearts and deeds

s: Rumi's story says correct belief about God doesn't matter
Musa was right that God has no body. the rebuke was for cutting the shepherd off.
a hadith in Sahih Muslim says God looks at your hearts and deeds, not your bodies or appearance
it stands behind the story's center: He looks at the heart.

games.q: after the masjid's kids' class, a little boy tells you God has a big white beard and lives on a cloud. his mom is nearby. what fits Musa's story?
o: smile, take his question seriously, and leave gentle teaching for later.
correct him right away so the wrong picture doesn't stick.
tell him anything he believes is fine, since only the heart counts.
games.why: the story keeps both halves: right belief matters, and correction must never cut someone off from God. Musa was sent to unite.

practice: Say one sentence out loud in the plainest words you own, no polish, no special language. If you pray, say it to God the way the shepherd did, as if to someone close; if not, say aloud one plain thing you're grateful for.
Then sit with how it felt to say it simply.

wordCard.voice: Musa and the shepherd: Rumi's story of a prophet who corrects a clumsy prayer and is told God looks at the heart.

orig.note: Arabic: heart; in the hadith, the place God looks.

carryVoice: For the clumsy prayers, yours and other people's: He looks at the heart. Four of Rumi's eight stories now.

sources.ref: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 2 (Moses and the shepherd)
Sahih Muslim 2564 (God does not look at your bodies or forms but at your hearts and deeds)
